justification_text:
My point estimates were anchored primarily to the prevailing price level of the asset at the time of the forecast, with modest upward drift built in across longer horizons. For the one-day estimate, I leaned heavily on recent price momentum and the tendency for short-term continuity in market prices — essentially assuming that absent a major catalyst, the price would remain close to its current level with only minor intraday variation. The one-week estimate incorporated a slight upward bias reflecting broader trend conditions, while the one-month estimate extended that drift further, assuming gradual appreciation consistent with longer-run trend assumptions. The incremental increases across horizons were intentionally small, reflecting my view that the asset was neither sharply oversold nor overbought at the time.

The width of the confidence intervals was calibrated to reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At the one-day horizon, the tight interval of roughly plus or minus twelve points reflects the relatively low realized volatility typical of short windows — barring scheduled macroeconomic announcements or surprise events, prices rarely move dramatically in a single session. By one week, the interval widens substantially to capture the possibility of meaningful directional moves driven by data releases, central bank commentary, or shifts in risk sentiment. The one-month interval is the widest, acknowledging that over a four-week period, multiple compounding uncertainties — macro data, geopolitical developments, earnings, and liquidity conditions — can collectively produce outcomes far from any starting point.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside even the relatively wide one-month interval. On the downside, a sharper-than-expected deterioration in macroeconomic data, a sudden tightening of financial conditions, or an escalation in geopolitical tensions could produce selling pressure well beyond what the lower bound captures. On the upside, a surprise dovish pivot from a major central bank, a strong risk-on catalyst such as better-than-expected corporate earnings, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical uncertainty could drive prices meaningfully above the upper bound. Liquidity events — such as a flash crash or a short squeeze — represent tail risks that are structurally difficult to price into any confidence interval and represent the most likely source of realized outcomes sitting outside the stated range.
